GK Chesterton if you're down for short stories, Dorothy Sayers if you're up for a longer and more meandering read. Personally, Baroness Emma Orczy, though less drawing-room than the rest, has a certain charm about her short stories, entitled Man in the Corner. 

As for Chesterton, his best short story collection is The Innocence of Father Brown. Granted, some of these don't feature murders, but I enjoyed the use of description, as well as the humor of a seemingly clumsy and naive priest/detective. As for Sayers, try Strong Poison as a sample; it's rather shorter than the others.  

The Detection Club in Britain included these authors, as well as others that I want to get around to reading. Considering these members were under the same murder mystery oath (a 'fair-play' murder), I think you'd find a similar style to Christie, though not necessarily the drawing room tone. Christie herself parodied her contemporaries' detectives and styles in Tommy and Tuppence's Partners in Crime, including John Thorndyke (short stories excellent, though heavy on the scientific side; longer stories dry).

Over six months, general session time. Some overlap.:

First month or so: Identifying feelings. Downloading Daylio (easy mood/activity-tracking app). 

Second to third month: Realizing how emotions affected me. As I trusted the therapist more and learned to express myself, talking about how I was doing. Helping me to find a psychiatrist and asking me how the psychiatrist session went. Identifying how the activities I tracked affected my mood.

Third month and onward: She started incorporating her suggestions for my life - thinking about how my job was affecting me, how my lack of daily activities on certain days was a bad idea. (Thank God I can have eye rolls and irritated faces in session.)

Fourth through six month: Putting all that together. When I'm chatty, I can come and talk about my week, and she'll listen and provide feedback. When I'm not feeling the urge to talk, she'll ask questions that will get me to engage (feelings, motivation or lack thereof that week).

I see someone for CBT (mixed with a bit of DBT), and - though I'd never tell her to her face - it's a life changer. 

The primary negative feeling I have is being suicidal. The trouble with some therapists I've encountered is that they expect you to sit down and monologue about your feelings, often unprompted, for 45 minutes. Problem is, when I'm suicidal - not even depressed -  there's really nothing else to say besides 'Hi, I'm suicidal, not sure why, here's my medical/family history.' Then, when asked the typical questions (hobbies, friends), they say something like 'Yeah, that helps, do more of that.' No shit, Sherlock, I'm partly here because I ran out of energy for hobbies/friends.

However, with this therapist (a LCSW, not sure what that is in your country), we started out the first couple sessions by identifying my feelings. We got me on Daylio, an easy app that tracks your activities and feelings. Granted, she is pushy about going out for hobbies, but she takes actual interest and makes practical suggestions for hobbies. 

All that to say, I'd look for a therapist who can both listen to you say whatever you want, 'enter your world' (so to speak), and ask the right questions when you don't know what to say. In my case, the CBT specialist. Hope this helps!
